text:
Image-only reading of the small pale guard

Orientation, staves, and surviving marks

I inspected all four supplied images. Images 001 and 002 supply binding context; the target is the small pale guard enlarged in images 003 and 004, not the more strongly written musical strip visible elsewhere in the overviews. The host volume's large title and numbers are not accompanying words of this guard.

Image 003 shows the pale guard upright in the displayed photograph, with the attachment at the bottom. Four short red, approximately horizontal line ends survive down its left edge, at roughly 30%, 45%, 60%, and 75% of image height. Their spacing supports a four-line musical staff, but almost all its horizontal extent has been cut away or is not visible on this face. There is no recoverable left-to-right musical run across the pale field.

At the left edge, around 10–16% of image width and 40–51% of image height, a dark upright sign straddles the second visible red line from the top. It has two vertically adjacent dark lobes or blocks and a thin, prolonged vertical stroke. It could be a clef-like sign, possibly C-shaped, but the surviving shape is insufficient for a secure clef identification. I can locate its center on that red line; I cannot securely identify a clef type, establish a musical reading direction from it, or assign absolute pitch. The two dark lobes should not automatically be counted as two successive sung notes.

Image 004 presents the guard with the attachment above and the surviving red line ends at the right. Its orientation is approximately reversed relative to image 003. The dark sign is near 60–64% of image width and 68–80% of image height. This looks like another view of the same surviving staff/sign area, not an independently surviving melodic passage. No sequence of separate noteheads extends into the pale field. Fold shadows, holes, sewing or attachment impressions, and scattered surface discoloration do not supply noteheads.

Relative pitch sequences

No continuous run can be responsibly transcribed from this guard. There are zero secure consecutive sung-note sequences of four notes, either before or after collapsing repeated pitches. Consequently I give no integer sequence: even a proposed pair such as [0, 1] would invent succession from the vertically arranged parts of a single ambiguous sign. There is no second usable passage.

Custos and text

The isolated marginal sign might alternatively contain a remnant of a note or guiding sign, including a custos, but neither a custos nor a sung note is securely distinguishable here. Its position alone does not settle this. No accompanying word or continuous letter group is legible on the pale guard. I therefore supply no literal word transcription and do not complete text from familiarity.

Coverage and limitations

Viewed image-001.jpg, image-002.jpg, image-003.jpg, and image-004.jpg. The actual detail images are visible and were inspected. The limitation is the extremely narrow survival of staff ends and an isolated ambiguous sign, with no exposed horizontal note succession, rather than an inability to open the images. The clear notes on the other, darker fragment in the overviews are outside this reading's assigned target.
